Then we count how many pupils fall in each bin. Each bar is one bin, and its height is the count. Our bars rise to a peak in the middle and fall away on both sides, like a hill. body.en:
A histogram shows how often values happen. Split the range into equal bins, such as 140–145 cm and 145–150 cm, count the values in each bin, and draw touching bars. The height of each bar is a count.

Look at the shape. A symmetric shape is a hill with two matching sides; heights often look like this, and the mean and median are close. A shape that is skewed right has most values on the left and a long tail to the right, like minutes spent on your phone: a few very large values pull the mean above the median.

The bin width is your choice. Too wide hides the shape; too narrow makes a spiky comb. Try more than one width before you describe the shape.

body.en:
Two classes can both have a mean mark of 12 and still be very different: in one, everyone scores 11 to 13; in the other, marks run from 5 to 19. The standard deviation (SD) measures this: it is roughly the typical distance of the values from the mean. A small SD means the values are close together; a large SD means they are spread out.

An outlier is a value far from the rest. One rule uses quartiles: Q1 is the value a quarter of the way up the ordered list, Q3 three quarters. The IQR is Q3 − Q1, and anything more than 1.5 × IQR below Q1 or above Q3 is flagged.

Never delete an outlier just because it is odd. A journey of 300 minutes might be a typing mistake for 30, or someone who really travels that far. Check it first.

transcript.en: A parent asked me: does sleep help my daughter's marks? I had sleep hours and test marks for our class. Two numbers for each pupil. How could I see if they go together? Today: scatter plots, correlation, and why together is not the same as cause. A scatter plot puts one measurement across and the other up. Each pupil becomes one dot. Sleep goes along the bottom, and the mark goes up the side. If the dots rise from left to right, that is a positive relationship. If they fall, it is negative, like screen time late at night and marks. If they make a shapeless cloud, there is no relationship. The correlation, called r, measures how close the dots are to a straight line. It goes from minus one to one. Near one is a strong positive pattern, near zero is no straight-line pattern. Here is a famous pattern. Ice cream sales and drownings rise together. Does ice cream make people drown? No. Hot weather brings both. So when sleep and marks go together, ask what else could explain it. Families with calm homes may give children both more sleep and more help with homework. Quick check! The dots lie very close to a rising straight line. Which r fits best? About zero point nine. Rising means positive, and close to a line means strong. Minus zero point nine would be a strong falling pattern. In the app, open Scatter, correlation and best fit. Tap to add pupils who study a lot but score low, and watch r fall. Your turn. Pupils with more books at home get higher marks, with r of zero point six. Does that prove books cause higher marks? No, not on its own. Remember: a scatter plot shows two measurements, r measures how close they are to a line, and correlation is not cause. Always ask what else could explain it. Try it yourself: measure the height and arm span of five people at home, and plot them. Is there a pattern, and does one really cause the other?

body.en:
A scatter plot shows two measurements for each person, one across and one up, with one dot per person. If the dots rise from left to right, the relationship is positive; if they fall, it is negative; a shapeless cloud means no straight-line relationship.

The correlation coefficient r measures how close the dots are to a straight line. It goes from −1 (a perfect falling line) through 0 (no line) to 1 (a perfect rising line). Values beyond about ±0.7 are usually called strong. One unusual point can change r a lot, so always look at the plot as well.

Correlation is not causation. Ice cream sales and sunburn rise together, but ice cream doesn’t burn you: hot sunny weather causes both. When two things go together, always ask what else could explain it.

يُظهر رسم الانتشار قياسين لكل شخص، أحدهما أفقيًا والآخر رأسيًا، بنقطة لكل شخص. فإذا صعدت النقاط من اليسار إلى اليمين كانت العلاقة موجبة، وإذا هبطت كانت سالبة، والسحابة بلا شكل تعني عدم وجود علاقة خطّية.

ويقيس معامل الارتباط r مدى قرب النقاط من خط مستقيم. ويمتد من −١ (خط هابط تام) مرورًا بـ ٠ (لا خط) إلى ١ (خط صاعد تام). وتُسمّى عادةً القيم التي تتجاوز نحو ±٠٫٧ قوية. وقد تغيّر نقطة غير معتادة واحدة r كثيرًا، فانظر دائمًا إلى الرسم أيضًا.

الارتباط ليس سببية. فمبيعات المثلّجات وحروق الشمس ترتفع معًا، لكن المثلّجات لا تحرقك: الطقس الحار المشمس يسبّب الاثنين. وحين يسير شيئان معًا، اسأل دائمًا عمّا قد يفسّر ذلك أيضًا.

transcript.en: Our school got a big table: attendance and marks for every class, for a whole year. Our class asked: where do we even start? We needed a routine. Today: a five-question routine for exploring any table of data. First, what is in it? Count the rows and columns. What is one row: a pupil, a class or a day? Which columns are numbers, and which are categories? Second, the shape. Draw a histogram of each number column. Is it a hill, or does it have a long tail? Third, the centre and the spread. Give the median and the range for skewed columns, and the mean and the standard deviation for symmetric ones. Fourth, gaps and oddities. Look for missing values, outliers and impossible numbers, like a class with one hundred and twenty percent attendance. Fifth, groups and relationships. Compare boys and girls, morning and afternoon, or villages. Draw a scatter plot of attendance and marks. Then ask the next question. Quick check! One class shows one hundred and twenty percent attendance. Which step of the routine catches this? Gaps and oddities. Attendance can't pass one hundred percent, so something went wrong, maybe pupils counted twice. Fix or flag it before you compare classes. Then write three findings, each with evidence. For example: attendance is lowest in the rainy months, with a median of eighty percent in July. A finding needs a number and where it came from. Your turn. Which is the better finding: attendance is bad, or attendance falls to a median of eighty percent in July? The second one: it has a number and a time. Remember the routine: what is in it, shape, centre and spread, gaps and oddities, groups and relationships. Then write findings with evidence. Try it yourself: pick a small table, like a week of weather, and go through the five questions. Write three findings with numbers, and one next question.

body.en:
Exploring data means getting to know it before you draw conclusions. Five questions work for almost any table. What is in it: how many rows, what is one row, which columns are numbers and which are categories? What shape: draw a histogram of each number column. Centre and spread: median and range for skewed columns, mean and SD for symmetric ones. Gaps and oddities: missing values, outliers, impossible numbers like 25 hours of sleep. Relationships: compare groups and draw scatter plots.

Then write findings. A good finding is specific and has a number: “On school nights I sleep a median of 7 hours; at weekends, 9” beats “I don’t sleep enough”. Finish with a next question, because exploring always leads to more questions.

def summary(xs):
    s = sorted(xs)
    return s[0], s[len(s) // 2], s[-1]
